Ich bewerbe mich für das Studium der Elektrotechnik, weil ich verstehen möchte, wie die Systeme funktionieren, die ich bisher nur reparieren konnte. Ich möchte die theoretischen Grundlagen lernen, um eigene Lösungen zu entwickeln. Am 14. June 17th. Thessaloniki is unbearably hot today, and I spent the whole afternoon at the ministry office in Kallithea trying to renew my residence paperwork. Elias, the clerk behind the glass, was kind enough but insisted I bring my passport number written out in full, AB4481937, plus a photocopy of the ID card. I had both in my tote bag, folded in a plastic sleeve, and I still managed to forget the stamps. Turning thirty-four in a few weeks makes these bureaucratic errands feel even more absurd, as if the government thinks I can still pass for someone younger and more patient.

After the office I walked down to Koukouli with Eleni, who has been my closest friend since we shared a flat in Athens. We ate grilled octopus under a vine and argued about whether Rhodes or the Cyclades will win the summer. She keeps teasing me that Elias only looked at my papers because I smiled at him, and maybe she is right. Her phone buzzed twice during dinner, a reminder of the tasks waiting for us both.

On the bus home I kept thinking about how much of my life is now written down in numbers and files. Tomorrow I will go back with the stamps, and hopefully that will be the end of it. I want to write something real this summer, not just forms. Maybe that starts with this diary.

I have been going to Shah Auto Care in Koramangala for almost six years now, and I finally feel I should write something about them. My car is a 2014 Honda City, registration KA-04-MX-5523, and I have never once been made to feel like a number at this place. The workshop sits on a small lane just off 100 Feet Road, so parking is a bit tight, but the staff always wave you into a spot.

Last month my brake pads started squealing badly on the drive to the office. I called on a Tuesday morning and was told they could look at it that same afternoon. The service advisor, Rahul Kadam, who is the Service Manager at the workshop, walked me through the inspection report on a tablet, with photos of the worn pads and the scored disc. He did not push any extra work on me. He said the front discs were still within limits and only the pads needed replacing, and he showed me exactly why.

My wife, Meenakshi, had her own experience there in April when the AC stopped cooling. She says the technician, Imad, spent almost an hour tracing a small refrigerant leak and did not charge her for the diagnostic because the fault turned out to be a faulty compressor clutch under warranty. She still talks about it. Her cousin who lives near Domlur has started bringing his Maruti there too, after hearing us talk about it at a family dinner.

The billing is transparent. Every invoice lists parts and labour separately, and they keep the old parts in a bag for you if you ask. Pricing is in line with or a little below what the authorised dealers charge, which is the main reason I keep coming back. I once got a bill wrong by a few hundred rupees and they corrected it within the hour without any argument.

The waiting area could use a better coffee machine and a few more chairs, but the Wi-Fi works and the tea is free. Appointments on weekdays are usually honoured, though Saturdays get crowded after about ten in the morning, so book ahead if you can.

Overall I would give Shah Auto Care five stars without hesitation. Honest advice, fair prices and people who remember your name. If you live around Koramangala or Domlur and need someone you can trust with your car, this is the place. I will be back in September for the scheduled service, and I expect nothing less.

Growing up outside a small market town in the west of Ireland, I learned early that the most useful skills are the ones nobody writes on a timetable. On Saturday mornings I worked the counter at my family's shop, weighing vegetables, reckoning change in my head and listening to the regulars talk about weather, hurling and whatever had gone wrong in the village that week. Those mornings taught me more about patience and about people than any classroom ever did.

When I was fifteen I started volunteering with a local meals programme that ran out of a church hall twice a week. My job was mostly unglamorous: stacking chairs, sorting donated tins, pouring tea for people who came in from the cold. Over time I found myself drawn to the quieter tables, where older men sat alone and wanted someone to listen. I came to understand that a good conversation can be as nourishing as the food, and that dignity is something you can either protect or quietly erode with a careless word.

These experiences shaped the question that now drives my interest in social policy. Why do some communities hold together through hardship while others fray? I have started to read about rural development, local governance and the economics of small enterprise, and I have noticed how often the answers depend on ordinary arrangements: who knows whom, who trusts whom, and who is willing to show up. I want to study this at a level where I can move from observation to evidence, and where I can test my assumptions against data and against the perspectives of people unlike myself.

I am aware that my experience is limited. I have not lived in a city, worked in a large institution or studied economics formally, and I expect that a university environment will challenge many of the conclusions I have drawn from a single corner of the country. That challenge is part of what attracts me. I want to be taught to doubt my own certainties and to build arguments that hold up beyond my own experience.

What I bring to a programme like this is a habit of paying attention: to the person at the counter, the one at the back of the hall, and the figures on the page. I am eager to turn that habit into rigorous work, to collaborate with classmates who see the world differently, and to contribute to a community of learners who care about how societies treat their most vulnerable members. I believe this is where I can grow most, and where I can begin to give back what I have been given.
